title: Check a found or frozen water filter
summary: A hollow-fibre or ceramic filter that froze, was dropped or comes with no history can look perfect and still let germs straight through. Use the maker's own test where there is one, treat the filter as broken if there's no test or it fails, and disinfect what comes out of it either way.

steps.text: Start from broken. A wet hollow-fibre filter that froze, or one with no history, counts as damaged until it passes its maker's test. Sawyer and LifeStraw say to replace one that may have frozen, and Katadyn warns a frozen membrane can let microorganisms through (Sawyer FAQ, LifeStraw temperatures, Katadyn BeFree manual).
Identify it: maker, model, and whether it's hollow fibre, ceramic or carbon. The test depends on the type, and only some makers give one (Katadyn change element, Sawyer FAQ).

Look it over in good light: cracked housings, split threads, missing or flattened O-rings and gaskets. Sawyer warns that overtightening damages gaskets and can start a hairline crack that widens (Sawyer FAQ).

Ceramic: take the element out and look for cracks or holes; any crack, however fine, means it goes (Katadyn old ceramic, Doulton FAQ). If it came with a thickness gauge, put one arm on each side of the ceramic: if the gauge stays in place the ceramic is thick enough, and if it slips, replace it (Katadyn old ceramic).

Katadyn BeFree: wet it with at least 2 L of clear water, squeeze the bottle until little water comes out, then, with the bottle held upright and the mouthpiece up, blow into the mouthpiece and keep blowing for at least 5 seconds (Katadyn BeFree test).

Read the bubbles: a steady stream of fine bubbles from the filter means a torn fibre, so it's broken. A few separate pea-sized bubbles are normal. If it fails, push another 2 L through and test once more (Katadyn BeFree test).

Sawyer: its filters can't be integrity-tested the way online videos show, and Sawyer says testing costs more than a new filter. It says to replace one that may have frozen, been boiled, dropped on something hard or overtightened, or came from an unauthorised seller (Sawyer FAQ).

Gravity units with candles or blocks (Berkey type): run the maker's red dye test. Add up to 1/8 teaspoon (10 drops) of artificial red food colouring per US gallon the system holds to the top chamber; pink or red water below means an element or plug isn't sealed, and clear water means the system is assembled correctly (Berkey elements). Berkey says the test is meant to confirm the system was assembled as intended, and that wet elements that freeze can crack or break (Berkey elements), so play safe and treat an element that froze as suspect even if the water stays clear.

Time the flow and clean or backflush as the maker says if it's slow (Sawyer FAQ, Doulton FAQ). Treat the flow as a hint only: it tells you about clogging, and Sawyer says there is no definitive way to tell whether freezing damaged a filter (Sawyer FAQ).
Write the result and date on the filter with tape and marker, so nobody trusts a failed one later.
steps.warn: Whatever the result, disinfect what comes out, and boil it if the filter failed or may have frozen: bleach and iodine work poorly on parasites. Filters of 0.3 micron or smaller don't stop viruses. Boiling or disinfecting can't make water with harmful chemicals safe (CDC hiking).

notes:
## Why a frozen filter is a trap
Hollow-fibre filters are bundles of fine tubes with walls full of tiny pores, and a used one holds water. LifeStraw says ice in the membrane can damage it badly enough to need replacing (LifeStraw temperatures); Sawyer says there is no definitive way to tell whether a wet filter was damaged by freezing, and recommends replacing it if you suspect it froze (Sawyer FAQ). The damage is inside the case, where you can't see it. In a Canadian winter, a used filter left overnight in a car, tent, porch or pack may well have frozen.

## What the makers say
| Maker | Freezing | Test they give | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sawyer (hollow fibre) | Rated 0–60 °C (32–140 °F); replace if you think it froze | Says integrity-test videos don't work on its filters; replace if frozen, boiled, dropped hard, overtightened or bought from an unauthorised seller | Sawyer FAQ |
| LifeStraw (hollow fibre) | Ice in a wet membrane can damage it; replace | | LifeStraw temperatures |
| Katadyn BeFree (hollow fibre) | BeFree Gravity manual: don't use in freezing conditions; a frozen membrane can let microorganisms through | Blow-through bubble test; replace if it fails or flow is badly restricted | Katadyn BeFree manual, Katadyn BeFree test, Katadyn change element |
| Katadyn ceramic | | Look for cracks; thickness gauge | Katadyn old ceramic, Katadyn change element |
| Doulton (ceramic candles) | | Inspect a dropped candle for cracks; replace if damaged | Doulton FAQ |
| Berkey (gravity elements) | Never let wet elements freeze: they can crack | Red food colouring test for leaks | Berkey elements |

Other makers have their own checks. Read the manual if you have it; if a maker gives no test and the filter may have frozen, retire it.

## How the bubble test works
A wet, intact membrane holds air back: water in the pores blocks it. A torn fibre lets air rush through as a stream of fine bubbles. That's why Katadyn's test only works on a well-wetted filter, needs 2 L or more through it first, and allows for the odd large bubble from the few fibres it builds in for air (Katadyn BeFree test). A dry filter, or one tested in a hurry, can fail for the wrong reason, so wet it and test twice before you write it off (Katadyn BeFree test).

## Ceramic candles
Ceramic is brittle. A crack lets dirty water bypass the ceramic (Katadyn change element), and Doulton says even small cracks can let contaminants through (Doulton FAQ). Inspect after any drop, and before using one that's been stored (Doulton FAQ). Katadyn says to replace a ceramic element before it gets too thin to filter well, and its gauge checks that (Katadyn change element, Katadyn old ceramic). Scrub gently with a soft brush or sponge under running water, no soap or detergent (Doulton FAQ).

Gaskets and wing nuts matter as much as the candle. A gravity unit whose candle seal leaks lets dirty water drip straight into the clean side. Berkey's red dye test is a leak test for exactly that: the elements and plugs are sealed if the water below stays clear (Berkey elements). Berkey also warns not to let wet elements freeze, as they can crack (Berkey elements).

## Flow rate: a hint, not proof
Slow flow often means a clogged filter: Sawyer says to backwash when flow drops (Sawyer FAQ), and Doulton says to clean the candle and replace it if cleaning doesn't restore flow (Doulton FAQ). Sawyer says there is no definitive way to tell whether freezing damaged a filter, so don't read normal flow as proof it's intact (Sawyer FAQ).

## Found filters
A filter found in a house, shop or car has an unknown history: it may have frozen, been dropped or be past its life. Sawyer's list of reasons to replace includes a filter bought from an unauthorised seller (Sawyer FAQ), and a found filter's origin is just as unknown. Sealed, never-used filters in their packaging are a different matter; it's the wet, used ones that freeze-damage hits (LifeStraw temperatures, Sawyer FAQ).

## Keeping one from freezing
Keep a used filter close to your body in the cold: in a pocket by day, in the sleeping bag at night (Sawyer FAQ, LifeStraw temperatures). At home, store it in a room that stays above freezing, and keep it on you if the house itself can drop below freezing.

## After any test, disinfect
No field test proves a filter is perfect, and most portable filters don't stop viruses: a 0.3 micron filter removes bacteria and parasites, but not viruses (CDC hiking); Sawyer's 0.1 micron filters don't remove viruses either (Sawyer FAQ). CDC's advice is to filter first, then disinfect (CDC hiking). If the filter failed, froze or has no history, boil: bleach and iodine don't work well on parasites, which a sound filter would have caught (CDC hiking). Otherwise boil, or use chlorine as in [Two-bucket gravity filter](#guides/build_gravity_water_filter). Boiling or disinfecting can't make water with harmful chemicals safe, and Katadyn says its BeFree doesn't remove chemicals (CDC hiking, Katadyn BeFree manual). See [Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters) for what each kind can and can't do.
